De lactuca. Ca. XXII.
Lactuca vt dicit Isidorus ex lactei humoris exuberantia est vocata. vel quia nutricientes mulieres lacte implet. hec in viris veneris motum arcet cuius duplex est species. scilicet domestica et agrestis qua feralia vocamus. quod dorsum eius aculeos habet duros ad modum ferre. vt dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. capitulo ultimo. de qua dicit Plinius in dietis. lactuca agrestis domestice in forma est similis. sed longiores habet frondes. subtiliores. asperiores. et minus virides. propter sue humiditatis paruitatem. et ideo multum est amaritudinis et ponticitatis respectu illius que domestica est. quia maioris est caloris et siccitatis. et ideo multi dicunt quod menstrua puocat et humores crudos expellit. vt dicit Dyascorides. lactuca pro domestica frigida est et humida secundum gradum et in neutra qualitate excedit modum. et ideo eius usus grauisui medicine. subtilibus subam et marie qui erit recens. et ideo cito digeritur et stomachi arsuram et morsuram et colera rubea sedat. sanguinis ebullitionem refrigerat. infomnietate placat. capitis dolorem et fumo colerico sanat. lac in mulieribus multiplicat et semen in viris generat augumentar. et accidit propter bonitatem sanguinis que gignit in pfecta quantitate. et in pfecta etate sed quando antiquatur et indurat minuitur eius humiditas et amaricat. et vsu eius sanguis pessimus generatur. virtus visina inde deficit et debilitatur. cuius causa est sensus animalis mortificatio. quod cum sua ponticitate ipsum suffocat naturale. et ideo talis lactuca generare voletib. maxime est nociua. nam materia gelat. coagulat seminale. et precipue semen eius si in cibo aut in potu sepe assumatur. De lappa. Ca. XXIII.
Lappa est herba habens folia lata et spissa circa terram habens in sumitatibus bastularum quedam capitella spinosa et aculeata sed recurua que vestibus transeuntium solent adherere. Vnde dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. lappa est dicta eo quod habeat caulez in gente terram dispositam et grecis philatropos vocatur. quod vestibus hominum adhereat ob asperitatem sui. et nascit iuxta muros. et ob philatropos. i. amans hominem. quia quadam affectione videat homis adherere vestibus. Lappe species duplex acuta et rotunda ad similitudinem pedis caballi disposita. vt a multis vocat vngula caballina. et vtriusque folia huis et horribilis sunt odoris pariter et saporis. vt dicit Dyascorides. Sed Plinius libro. xxvi. lappe multe sunt species et omnes sunt medicinales. Regarding Lettuce. Chapter XXII.
Lettuce, as Isidore says, is named from the abundance of its milky humor, or because it fills nursing women with milk. This plant restrains the movement of lust in men. There is a twofold species of it, namely domestic and wild, which we call <term>feralia</term> <gloss>wild/brutal plants</gloss>, because its back has spines that are hard like iron, as Isidore says in book XVII, in the last chapter. Regarding this, Pliny says in his treatises on diet: "Wild lettuce is similar in form to the domestic, but it has longer, thinner, rougher, and less green leaves due to the scarcity of its moisture, and therefore it has much bitterness and astringency compared to the domestic, because it is of greater heat and dryness." And therefore many say that it provokes menstruation and expels raw humors, as Dioscorides says. Lettuce, specifically the domestic kind, is cold and moist according to the degree, and it does not exceed the limit in either quality. Therefore, its use is beneficial for medicine, <unclear>subtle, and fresh</unclear> <note>The OCR is unclear here; the sense suggests it is beneficial when fresh.</note> and therefore it is quickly digested; it calms burning and biting in the stomach and red bile, cools the boiling of the blood, appeases sleeplessness, and heals headache and choleric vapor. It increases milk in women and creates and augments semen in men, and this occurs because of the goodness of the blood which it produces in perfect quantity and at a perfect age. But when it grows old and hardens, its moisture is diminished and it becomes bitter, and by its use, very bad blood is generated. The vital faculty fails and is weakened from it, the cause of which is the mortification of the animal sense, because with its astringency it suffocates the natural heat. And therefore, such lettuce is most harmful to those wishing to procreate, for it congeals and coagulates the material of semen, and especially its seed if it is frequently taken in food or drink, says Isaac in his treatises on diet. Moreover, Pliny in book XX, chapter VIII, says about lettuce: "There is a species of lettuce growing spontaneously which they call goat lettuce, which, when brought into the sea, kills fish that are in the vicinity, and whose stem and leaves, when rubbed with salt, heal wounded nerves. There is another species of lettuce that grows in fields, whose leaves, when crushed with pearl barley and applied as a poultice, heal ulcers, and the Greeks call this <term>ysopon</term> <gloss>hyssop</gloss>. A third species is that which grows in woods, which they call <term>steraton</term> <gloss>wood-lettuce</gloss>, whose leaves, when crushed with fat, heal wounds. With its root and leaves, it mitigates the holy fire <note>referring to ergotism or erysipelas</note>. There is also another species of this lettuce that is round and short, which many call <term>beratia</term> <gloss>borage/variety of lettuce</gloss>, whose juice, when hawks are scratching their eyes..."

<column-break/>

"...and those who apply it to their eyes, dispel obscurity and dimness when they age. The juice of this herb heals the eyes and the sea <note>likely a misreading of 'serpents' or an error in the original text</note>, and to it, one mixes human milk. It cures the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions if its juice is drunk with wine and its crushed leaves are applied over the wound as a plaster. It also dispels and suppresses every swelling. The seed of lettuce, both wild and domestic, suppresses imaginations of lust in sleep, and does not allow the body to be polluted if it is frequently taken in food. However, its frequent and excessive use causes darkness in the eyes. Pliny attributes many other praises to it in the same chapter, but these suffice."

Regarding Burdock. Chapter XXIII.
Burdock is an herb having broad and thick leaves near the ground, having at the tips of its stalks certain thorny and prickly heads, but curved, which are accustomed to adhere to the clothes of passersby. Whence Isidore says in book XVII: "Burdock is so named because it has a stalk arranged near the ground, and it is called <term>philatropos</term> <gloss>human-loving</gloss> by the Greeks, because it adheres to the clothes of men due to its roughness, and it grows near walls; and it is called <term>philatropos</term>, i.e., loving man, because with a certain affection it seems to adhere to the clothes of a man." There is a double species of burdock, acute and round, arranged in the likeness of a horse's foot, so that by many it is called <term>vngula caballina</term> <gloss>coltsfoot</gloss>, and the leaves of both are of a horrible odor and taste alike, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny says in book XXVI: "There are many species of burdock and all are medicinal. For they cure the stings of scorpions, nor do they strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice. A decoction of its root helps the teeth and also strengthens them if it is held warm in the mouth. Its seed taken internally cures ailments of the stomach; it is useful for those vomiting blood and it assists in cases of dysentery; for its root taken with wine stops the flow of the bowels. But when given alone, it helps those with stones <note>kidney stones</note>. The whole herb crushed with lard is good for swellings." The verdict of Pliny, according to Platearius: burdock or dock is a warm and dry herb having the power of dissolving, relaxing, opening, and attenuating, and therefore it is valid against scabies, itching, herpes, and impetigo, and it draws out humors from the skin. It dissolves the hardness and swelling of abscesses; it is effective against cold dropsy and obstruction of the spleen. Its juice, when mixed with rue, purges the brain and rheumatic flow if taken in small quantity.

XXXIII. Concerning Imaginary Time, we judge the same as we do concerning Imaginary space, namely, that beyond the intrinsic durations of things, which establish diverse relations of distance and proximity, it is in reality nothing at all.

XXXIV. Finally, duration is either created or uncreated. The uncreated belongs to GOD alone, and is called Eternity; and it is defined by <term>Boethius</term>: *The simultaneous and perfect possession of an interminable life.* Created duration is either temporary or perpetual. Temporary is that which has both a beginning and an end. Perpetual is that which, at the least, has no end. Such is the duration of Angels and the rational soul, which is also called <term>Aevum</term> <gloss>an intermediate duration between time and eternity</gloss>, and is commonly defined as: *The interminable permanence of a thing in a state of being once received.*

### ON QUANTITY.

XXXV. <term>Aristotle</term> describes a quantity here in book 5, text 18: *That which is divisible into those things which are contained within it, of which each one is a certain one, and is suited to be a "this something."* That is to say (as Father <term>Suarez</term> interprets it), those things of which each is suited by its own nature, through itself, to remain as one certain whole, separated from others; and indeed, insofar as it is by the force of quantity, it is divisible in the same way, namely by physical and natural divisibility, by the power of which one body naturally expels another, or its parts, from the place they occupied before.

XXXVI. There is an opinion, as Father <term>Suarez</term> says, sufficiently common among the <term>Thomists</term>, that the primary formal effect of quantity is the distinction of integral parts; so that without quantity, neither prime matter nor any other material entity would have any integral parts. Following our own, Father <term>Vasquez</term> (Vol. 3, on Part 3, d. 190, from no. 20) followed the <term>Thomists</term>. But on the contrary: 1. Just as each thing is an entity through itself, so it is one through itself, and consequently divided and distinct from anything else. 2. Because otherwise one would have to proceed to infinity. For if one thing is distinct from another by a third entity, then it would have to be distinguished from that third by a fourth, and so on to infinity. 3. Because matter is presupposed for quantity with its entire entity. Therefore it cannot receive parts from it; for since a whole is nothing other than all its parts, that which is presupposed with its entire entity must also be presupposed with its parts. Therefore, the primary formal effect of quantity cannot consist in the distinction of parts.

the union of the body, with the harmony of its members under one spirit, constitutes the form of society; the intention of living well holds the proximate final cause; but the desire to arrive at a future state holds the final intention, for the sake of which other things are established. From all this, the necessity of an administration is gathered, which might correspond to this intention, lead it to effect, and preserve it. It is taught that a sovereignty, as if it were a single Spirit, and the art of ruling, is required no less than in a single physical body. Reason in the soul is the intellect of things to be done, and of those things which must be delegated to be executed by individual members. The members of a single human are not suitable for all actions, but must be preserved and informed under their proper functions. A foot cannot see, an eye cannot walk, an ear cannot touch, a hand cannot hear, because it lacks the instrument or organ for that purpose. Nor does the soul, which knows the faculty and action of each member, order the same thing, but it commands what is proper; and thus it entirely cares for individual things with its own solicitude. Prudent administration, which presides over the body of society, follows this example; it foresees and provides for what is suitable for individual members, or men. First and primarily, it looks to the whole body of the people, and then also to individuals; lest, while it considers only the universal, and neglects the parts from which the whole is perfected, the whole itself should fail.

And here "people" has a broader significance than that of a college, a town, or a city, though the multitude of these is also called a people; but with a demonstration of particularity applied, as we say the people of the city of Toulouse, or the people of another place. The canons also have spoken of "people" as the plebs, or the number of parishioners of a certain parish, even if there were only ten men gathered together.

<margin>b l.16. concerning those who are permitted, that the "what of each" is not of the universal. c Nicolaus Perrotus on the 2nd epigram of Martial, in "Cornucopiae" §. plebiscite, concerning natural law.</margin>
This, however, is not properly admitted, but is spoken of as if by the likeness of universal society, as the example of the republic has been said by some to be permitted to possess a civil body.

<margin>l.2. §. "deinde cum difficile," concerning the origin of law. P.</margin>
12 The name "people" contains more than "plebs." Plebs is said to be from <term>πλήθειον</term> <gloss>multitude</gloss>, from the many. But "people," from <term>πολλῶν πλειόνων</term> <gloss>from the much more numerous</gloss>, because the people is completed by all orders of men, as we shall say. Thus, in the common tongue in France, we also say "le peuple" for the universal congregation and society of men, and we call the plebs "le menu populaire," or "menu peuple," which some call by contempt, "la populace."

<margin>d §. 1. concerning public judgments, in the works of Justinian. Alicia on l."bona ciuitatis," concerning the meaning of words. P. e Heading concerning popular actions. P. l."eū qui," in popular actions, concerning oaths. P. f l.1. §. "quies quoque," concerning the office of the urban prefect. P.</margin>
12 From "people" <term>populus</term>, "public" <term>publicum</term> is derived: as if it were <term>popublicum</term>, that which pertains or can pertain to all the people. Popular actions, which are also called public; and "popular sacrifices," as Festus and Labeo say, are those which all citizens perform, and which are not attributed to certain families, as the <term>fornicalia</term> <gloss>festival of the ovens</gloss> and the <term>palilia</term> <gloss>festival of Pales</gloss> were. Hence "popular and public peace," of all subjects.

Formerly, the letter O was pronounced for U in many words, just as even today Italians and Germans are accustomed to pronounce a thick U for O or OU. they were cleansed from their sins. But those others once heard <note>continuing from the previous page: "what we sing"</note>, they received signs. For this reason, signs were given to them, as a sword of salvation preaching. Thus, the sign was not given to all the foreigners, so that it might cut through by the word. So too Paul says: "Not to all who believe, but to the unbelievers." You see that the gift <term>charisma</term> <gloss>gift/grace of the Spirit</gloss> is not for us from the Lord, but for those others, those ignorant of the word of the Lord, so that he may teach them. For wishing to welcome the faith, he preaches without another; and these signs are their signs, that this body may be built up. For if we had not first received signs and preached, we would not have believed in Him. Since, therefore, they received signs, and without this [we would not], all the way was hidden. This, therefore, is the cause that signs do not happen now. The orator wishes to speak from God in a way worthy of the feast, and also what is the reason for the Pentecost; and why in this feast the gift is given; and why in tongues of fire; and why after ten days. But it is because at Pentecost the teaching from the law is [fulfilled]; therefore, I will add a little,

<column-break/>

and I will rest the discourse. "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire." Not fire, but *like* fire, so that you might not suspect anything sensible regarding the fire. For just as at the Jordan stream, a dove did not descend, but *like* a dove, so too here. Not fire, but *like* fire. And again, a little less [is said] regarding that which is as a rushing mighty wind.

But for what reason does Ezekiel not receive the gift of prophecy through something like fire, but through a book? And the apostles receive the grace through fire? In vain; for my Lord says to me: "And he gave into my mouth the scroll of the book; and it was written, the things written, and a lamentation, and woe, and a sea monster; the things behind [were] written after the things in front; and I ate it; and it became in my mouth as honey, sweetening." But regarding the apostles, it is not so; but "there appeared unto them tongues like as of fire." For what reason, then? There [it was] letters, but here tongues and fire; because my Lord was alone in condemning sins.

...upon the seal and stripping it of the garments of forms entirely, delaying from its time, for it only appears in the emergence of the one who is the <term>Paraclete</term> <gloss>comforter or messenger</gloss> and the manifestation of his specific sainthood. Even if it is unveiled, because <term>seal-prophecy</term> <gloss>the final prophecy</gloss> itself is in the most complete state within the emergence of prophecy, such that it is folded within its brilliance. It <note>referring to the seal</note> was upon its symbolic naming, and no forms remained upon it. For the Truth has subtle essences that manifest in, and the remainder of them is the beauty of those Truths. Therefore, the <term>Paraclete</term> said all the prophets and the uncovering are truths of their prophets, but some of those manifestations remained. Thus, the requirements of prophecy are suspended, entrusted to the unveiling of the manifestations of his specific sainthood, observing what is appropriate for the readiness of the time. There is no doubt that the <term>lights of the kingdom</term> <gloss>divine realms</gloss> are descending, not having a limit for those who touch them, with no prevention in them, and that the <term>ray of the holy</term> <gloss>divine radiation</gloss> spreads upon the prepared, detached souls. The path of Truth opens for those who knock at its door, meaning that the door of God is open. For the <term>Bestower of Knowledge</term> <gloss>God</gloss>, who is at the <term>highest horizon</term> <gloss>the ultimate cosmic boundary</gloss>, is not stingy with the unseen. In it, meanings appear with a rank, as if it is more hidden to the possessor of intelligence, just as the <term>Preserved Tablet</term> <gloss>the divine register</gloss> has informed us. "Preserved" in language: its verb is from "hifz," meaning to snatch away. The intended meaning here is a subtle unseen from the <term>world of the senses</term> <gloss>the manifest, physical realm</gloss>. <note>The</note> extinguished lights are unsteady, not fixed, following a flashing light upon the soul on the night of the "al-Nu'uj" <note>a metaphorical storm or tempest</note>. It is in the language the violent wind that uproots houses. The intended meaning here is the hardship leading to the rejection of bodily powers, and that is not achieved except by the blowing of the winds of attractions from the highest source, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Glad tidings to whoever sends the winds as a herald before His mercy." The easy path—he is in it, meaning a moment from its owner, meaning the owner of the preservation, descending, and in him is the return from the light, ascending from him the image of that witnessing.

<summary>This passage discusses the nature of the Paraclete as the manifestation of final prophecy and specific sainthood, emphasizing the transition from physical forms to the unveiling of divine truths through spiritual receptivity.</summary>

infuse into the <term>maceres</term> <gloss>soaked substances</gloss>, as those with <term>sinancici</term> <gloss>quinsy/throat inflammation</gloss> are accustomed to gargle usefully; that is, only pure <term>palmulas caricas</term> <gloss>dried dates and figs</gloss>, boiled in a mixture of sweet <term>cantabro</term> <gloss>a type of bran-based gruel or drink</gloss>, so that you may drink it, or also other similar things which are collected in the <term>farmacoutici</term> <gloss>pharmacopoeia</gloss> individually and described properly according to their own cause, and they should be used in their own time. It is necessary to know how to cut, and to which places those that suffer should be applied. Thus, one might be able to know where <term>antispasis</term> <gloss>revulsion (drawing blood or humors away from an affected part)</gloss> and when you ought to perform it for a cause, such as <term>metocheuresis</term> <gloss>derivation (drawing humors toward a part)</gloss>. For <term>antispasis</term> is a counter-evacuation; for example, if humors are flowing from the thigh or from some other part of the body, I will soon open a vein in the arm, and by pulling the humors toward the heart, I will intercept the rising cause. Or I will place cups <note>original: "cũēbras"; cupping glasses</note> on the breast, so that it may draw them up. I will cause it to be rubbed by hand, or I will constrict the joints of the hands with ligatures. <term>Metocheuresis</term> is the redirection of humors; when there is a descent, I will take away blood by opening a vein in the sole of the foot or the ankle, and by leading it toward a lower part, I will derive it, and I will purge the place and the sense, so that I apply cups to the place which is in pain, and I will warm and rub both, and constrict them with ligatures.

If, therefore, the right side of the womb or the body suffers, I will draw blood from the right arm or the right leg, opening any vein that is internal or that is of the proper member which is suffering. If, however, the left side suffers, it is necessary to draw blood from the left arm or leg. Likewise, if the liver is lower, I will take blood from the right arm; if the spleen, from the left, opening the internal vein. If some upper part of the body is suddenly afflicted by heat, such as in the throat of those with <term>sinancici</term> <gloss>quinsy</gloss>, and of the eyes, or [in cases of] fever or impulse, and sudden pains, we draw blood from those same higher parts, whether by <term>antispasis</term> or by <term>metocheuresis</term>, and I will provide a purgative, carefully considering the reason and quality of the hours, and also the enema, as the cause of the lifestyle requires. If these are applied usefully to the beginning, it is well. But if the cause is <term>chronia</term> <gloss>chronic</gloss>, that is, already inveterate, then it is better for blood to be removed from the suffering place or member itself. 

Thus we also incise veins under the tongue for those with <term>sinancici</term> <gloss>quinsy</gloss>, when the time for evacuation has arrived, as the experts have indicated, and nevertheless we provide the cause [and] diet for a long time. For the spleen and the liver itself, we apply cups to the side with a scalpel, and we purge any other place by scarifying, when the cause of the lifestyle is already becoming <term>chronia</term> <gloss>chronic</gloss>, and there is now no humor flowing in it. Otherwise, if it is done differently, I would not say it will be helped by the fruits, but rather [that it will be] much harmed. That, however, before all else must be considered: that we know the quality or virtue of the medicines and the nature of the places or members themselves which are suffering. For some of them feel [effects] slowly and endure the virtue of the medicines for a long time. Some feel them soon and do not endure them for long. Therefore, limbs that feel quickly are indignant at benefit applied with vehemence and sharpness, more than they are healed, if they are applied harshly or beyond measure.
